full_judgment:
2. The relevant facts for disposal of this civil appeal, in short, are that present appellant as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No.65 of 1997 for pre-emption of the case land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 [in brief the Act] in the Court of Assistant Judge, First Court, Kalia, Narail, stating, inter alia, that the preemptor is a co-sharer in the case holding by purchase. Afsaruddin Bhuiyan, father of the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee was owner of 1.10 acre land in the case holding by purchase vide registered deed No.4009 dated 13.05.1970. The pre-emptor also purchased 0.20 acre land-from the case holding by a registered deed dated 17.06.1982 from one Rakib Biswas who purchased the same with other land from the heirs of recorded owners. By this way, the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the case holding. On the other hand, the pre-emptee is a stranger in the case holding, who purchased the case land from his father, Afsaruddin Bhuiyan vide registered deed No.5416 doted 14.12.1995 at a consideration of taka 12,000.00 beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor without serving any notice as required under section 89 of the Act. After the death of Afsaruddin, on 01.06.1997, the pre-emptor came to know that his father transferred the case land to the pre-emptee. Then, the pre-emptor obtained certified copy of the said deed on  10.06.1997. He is a cultivator and not owner of more than 10 bigha land. Hence, he filed this pre-emption application. 

 15. In the present case, the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below has arrived at concurrent finding that the pre-emption petition is not barred by limitation. But the trial Court as well as the appellate Court did not appreciate the evidence of the witnesses of the petitioner on the point of the date of knowledge of the impugned sale deed though the present pre-emption petition was filed almost 1 year 8 months later from the date of impugned sale deed. The trial Court with-out appreciating the evidence of the witnesses on record in that regard came to a conclusion that though the petitioner deposed some inconsistent statements regarding knowledge of the impugned sale deed, it was not proved that he knew about the impugned sale deed earlier and the pre-emption petition is not time barred since the petitioner filed the petition with-in the prescribed period of limitation. The appellate Court went a step forward and without appreciating the evidence of the witnesses of petitioner on record with respect to the date of knowledge of the impugned sale deed decided that the petition was not time barred since the opposite party did not give notice of the impugned sale to the petitioner and the consent of the petitioner to the impugned sale deed was not proved. Both the Courts below did not take into account the legal proposition that as per section 96(1) of the Act read with sec ions 101 and 103 of the Evidence Act, 1872, the burden of proof as to the date of knowledge of the impugned sale deed is with the petitioner to prove that he has filed the pre-emption petition within 4 months from the date of knowledge of the impugned sale deed. The trial Court as well as the appellate Court should have been very much cautious in addressing the point of limitation. The right of pre-emption being a feeble right requirements of law have to be fully complied with to be entitled to pre-emption. A citizen's right to deal with his property freely, in view of the special statutory provision, bears a clog, that is, subject to right of pre-emption. The statutory provision providing such a right curtailing owner's right to deal with his property must be construed very strictly [Ahmed Hossain and others-Vs-Basharat Ali and others 32 DLR (AD) 54].The claim of pre-emption is a predatory right and that is why, the legislature has imposed conditions for claiming pre-emption, such as, the petition should be made within four months of the service of notice under section 89, or if no notice has been served, within four months of the date of knowledge of the transfer. Even if the pre-emptee does not raise the above point, the requirement of law must be satisfied by the pre-emptor before claiming a right of pre-emption [Habibur Rahman Bhuiyan and others-Vs-Galman Begum and Others, 64 DLR AD page 133]. The petitioner came to Court to enforce a right. A period of limitation is prescribed by the statute for the purpose. The burden lies with him to prove the date of his alleged knowledge and that is within the period of limitation. On a consideration of the language used in section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, it further appears that the definite article "the" has been used to qualify "knowledge" occur-ring twice in the section. It, therefore, indicates that "the knowledge" must by definite knowledge. A precise or exact perception of the necessary particulars of a fact is the determinant of "the knowledge" which is essentially a question of fact [Habibur Rahman Khalifa-Vs-Satish Chandra Ghose 29 DLR 178]. When a pre-emptor is coming to the court to exercise his right of preemption, which is essentially a predatory right, after a long lapse of time a heavy duty is cast upon him to prove his alleged knowledge about the impugned sale by most convincing evidence so as to circumvent the bar of limitation [Habibur Rahman alias Md. Habibur Rahman and another-Vs-Mobarak All Rani and others, 50 DLR 193]. 

 16. Now, let us proceed to ascertain whether the interference by the High Court Division with the finding of the courts below regarding the point that the petition is not barred by limitation is justified or not. The petitioner stated in the pre-emption petition that he for the first time came to know about the impugned sale deed on 01.06.1997 A.D. corresponding to ১৮ জ্যেষ্ঠ ১৪০৪ বাংলা সাল. The petitioner did rot depose in his examination-in-chief the corresponding Gregorian calendar date when he knew about the peti-impugned sale deed. Though the petitioner PW-1 deposed in his examination-in-chief, "পিতা মারা গেলে ১৪০৪ সালের ১৮ই জ্যেষ্ঠ তর্কিত দলিলের কথা বলে ও দখল ছেড়ে দিতে বলেচ, he deposed during his cross-examination, "১৪০৪ সালে বিক্রয়ের কথা জানি। ১৪০৪ সাল বাংলা না ইংরেজি তা বলিতে পারিনা। বর্তমানে বাংলা কত সাল তা বলিতে পারিনা"। If we go through this portion of the deposition of Pw-1, we find that he failed to prove definitely that he knew occur-about the impugned sale deed for the first time on 18th Jaishtha 1404 BS. Pw-2 deposed in cross-examination, "১৪০৪ সালের জ্যেষ্ঠ মাসে একরাম প্রকাশ করে। আমি বাংলা কোন সালে বিবাহ করি তা স্মরণ নাই। আমার সর্বশেষ সন্তানের জন্ম কত তারিখ তা মনে নাই।" Pw-2 also failed to corroborate the testimony of Pw-1 on the point of the date of knowledge of the impugned sale deed since he did not cate-exergorically mention the date when he exactly heard about the impugned sale deed. Pw-3 deposed, "মতিয়ার আমাকে বলে নালিশী জমি একরাম দলিল করে নেয়। কোন দাগের জমি বা ফাহার নিকট থেকে লিখে নেয় সে সম্পর্কে আমাকে কিছু বলে নাই। কথা শুনে আমি চলে যাই। অন্য কোনো বিষয় আমি জানিনা। কোন তারিখে একরাম বা মতিয়ার বলে তা বিবরণ নেই।" Pw-3 was not told which property or whose property was taken by the Opposite party Ekram. Moreover, Pw-3 did not depose when he heard about the impugned sale deed. on the point of the date of knowledge c the petitioner about the impugned gale deed for the first time, the evidence definite of the petitioner's witnesses is not definite, complete, corroborative and convincing enough to dis-charge his burden of proof. "Knowledge" as referred to in sub-section 1 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act means and includes a definite and complete knowledge in order to qualify the petitioner to file an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act[Abdul Sattar and another-Vs-Osimuddin and Others, 42 DLR 24).The High Court Division accepted the evidence of OPWs regarding the point that the transfer was within the knowledge of the petitioner since OPW-1, Ekram Hossain, who is also full brother of pre-emptor Motiar Rahman and OPW-2, Atiar Rahman, who is also full brother of pre-emptor Matiar Rahman and OPW-3 Karim Sheikh, Sister's husband of the pre-emptor, all these OPWs testified in one voice that their father late Afsaruddin transferred the case land to the preemptee opposite party by a registered kabala dated 14/12/1995 within full knowledge of all his sons arid daughters including the pre-emptor. The High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment of the courts below when the same has been made either upon mis-reading or non-consideration of the material evidence and the said mis-reading and non-consideration of the evidence caused failure of jus-tice [Habibullah (Md)-Vs-Sher Ali Khan and others, 57 DLR (AD) 55]. The High Court Division is empowered to interfere with the findings of fact if the findings are perverse or there has been a non-appreciation or non-consideration of the material evidence on record by the Courts below [Masjid kacha Tank, Nahan-Vs-Tuffail Mohammed, AIR 1991 SC 455]. 

 No.1 as Opw-1 deposed, "নালিশী জমিসহ ১.১০ একর জমি আমার পিতা ১৯৭০ সালে খরিদ করে দখল করিত। বাবা এর পরবর্তীতে ৯৮ শতক জমি ১৪/১২/৯৫ তারিখে রেজিঃ কবলামূলে আমার নিকট বিক্রয় করে। বক্রি ১২ শতক জমি ভোগ দখলকালে বাবা মারা গেলে আমরা সবাই উত্তরাধিকার লাভ করি। সেই হিসাবে আমি ও প্রার্থী শরীক।" It transpires from this portion of the deposition of the opposite party No.1 that the impugned deed was registered on 14/12/95 and the opposite party No.1, after his father's death, became a co-sharer tenant in the holding by inheritance subsequent to the registration of the impugned deed No.5416 dated 14/12/95. At the date of registration of the impugned deed No.5416 dated 14/12/95 opposite party No.1, Md. Ekram Hossen, was not a co-sharer tenant in the holding by inheritance. It is now a well settled principle of law that the cause of action under section 96 of the State Acquisition and' Tenancy Act accrues on the date of the registration of the deed of sale, when registration is compulsory [Ayesha Khatun (Musammat)- Vs-Musammat Jahanara Begum and others, 43 DLR (AD)9). The right of pre-emption accrued to the pre-emptor is not affected by the subsequent acquisition of co-sharership by the pre-emptee [Abdul Baten-Vs-Abdul Latif Sheikh and others, 45 DLR (AD) 26]. One who acquires co-sharership subsequent to the dare of notice of transfer or one who becomes a co-sharer in the holding on a date later to the date of presentation of the deed of transfer for registration and sought to be pre-empted is not competent to oppose pre-emption [Fatema Khatun and others-Vs-Abdul Quddus 58 DLR (AD)110]. From this perspective of the case, we hole that the impugned sale to the pre-emptee is not protected from pre-emption under sub-section 10(a) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The High Court Division probably did not analyze this aspect of this case. However, this finding does not have any impact upon the decision of the case since the petition is barred by limitation.
